messages.subject: Re: [seewave] help understanding the timer function
messages.body_plain:
Hello Eric,

timer() is a rather simple function that tries to take appart signal and no-signal sections in a sound sample.

There are two main parameters for selection: an amplitude threshold (argument 'threshold', evrying above this threshold is considered as signal) and a time threshold (argument 'dmin', everything above this threshold is considered as signal). These both threshold work on the amplitude envelope that might be a bit noisy. One solution to smooth this amplitude envelope is to apply a moving average. The process of moving average is based on the definition of a sliding window with potential overlap between successive windows. An average of the amplitude is computed for each window slided along the amplitude envelope. I think you should be able to find documentation on the web on this process which is commonly used in time series analysis.

For your example, that has a good SNR, an amplitude threshold of 2% seems to be appropriate but the envelope is a bit complex such that you need to smooth it quite a lot with a moving average based on a 400 sample window. To help the process we can also specify that there are no volcalizations shorter than 0.1 s with the argument 'dmin':

> t0 <- timer(w, threshold=2, msmooth=c(400,0), dmin=0.1)

However, be aware that the moving average process does a kind of downsampling than can affect the precision of the time measurements. You can limit this by specifyng an overlap between the successive windows, here set to a quite high value of 90%:

> t0 <- timer(w, threshold=2, msmooth=c(400,90), dmin=0.1)

We can now look at the results:

> t0
$s
[1] 2.3390272 0.1553296 0.2252733 0.6313103 0.1171785 0.4341961 0.1126367

$p
[1] 0.71942119 0.13897909 0.15351285 0.38060288 0.12807877 0.00181672 0.77846459

$r
[1] 1.744966

$s.start
[1] 0.000000 3.058448 3.352757 3.731543 4.743456 4.988714 5.424726

$s.end
[1] 2.339027 3.213778 3.578030 4.362853 4.860635 5.422910 5.537363

$first
[1] "signal"

The total duration of the vocalizations seems to be correct

> sum(t0$s)
[1] 4.014952

The average and sd of the vocalization duration are
> mean(t0$s)
[1] 0.5735645
> sd(t0$s)
[1] 0.8017259

Unfortunately there is no magic tool to find optimal parameters for a long list of sound samples, in particular if the quality of the samples differ significantly. I guess this might be a bit risky to do it totally blindly and I would suggest to check at least some samples to estimate potential errors.

HTH

Jerome

>
> t0 <- timer(w, threshold=5)

>
> t1b <- timer(w, threshold=5, msmooth=c(10,0), dmin=0.03)
> sum(t1b$s)
> # [1] 0.05419851
>
> t2b <- timer(w, threshold=5, msmooth=c(20,0), dmin=0.03)
> sum(t2b$s)
> # [1] 0.1483142
>
> Thanks!
> Eric

Dear Jerome,

This is a very helpful explanation. Thanks a lot for taking the time to write such a thoughtful reply.

I have a much better sense now of what you mean by windows to calculate a moving average. And your mention of time series analysis helped me to think of points as data points (e.g., weekly, monthly, etc).

I hope this is not a really dumb question, but I am still a bit confused about how to establish the number of points for the smoothing. You suggested a sample window of 400. Would you mind saying a bit more about how you arrived at this suggestion? I think having more insight into this decision will help me to evaluate the rest of my files.

(A side question is how to determine the total points in a time series like this wave. Is this equivalent to the number of samples in the wave object...in this case 278,528).

If you have time, I'd also be very interested to know your thoughts about when one should use msmooth vs ssmooth. I read an answer you gave to someone else noting that ssmooth does not down sample.

Thanks again for your help, and for the great package of course.

Eric

messages.body_plain:
Hi Pedro,

There are two immediate problem I see is with the code:

1) for (i in (length(temp_param$s)))
This only iterates over one value: the length of temp_param$s
I think you mean:
  for(i in 1:length(temp_param$s))
Which iterates over 1 through the length of temp_param$s

2) spec_param[,] <- dfreq(...)
As far as I know, this tells R to save the output of dfreq as an object called spec_param. Although you specify [,] this doesn't actually mean anything, so this is why spec_param only has the last iteration saved.

I'm also confused as to what you hope to get in the end... your matrix is 12 x the length of temp_param$s, but you're only taking 10 dfreq samples, right? Also, why only have only two columns in your matrix, as opposed to the number of calls in your wave file (length(temp_param$s))?

As it looks as if you are taking 10 dfreq measurements at different spots in "call.wav", I would suggest using a data frame:

spec_param <- expand.grid(wave_file = "call.wav", call = temp_param$s, sample = 1:10,  dfreq = NA)
for (i in 1:length(temp_param$s)) {
  spec_param$dfreq[spec_param$call == temp_param$s[i]] <- dfreq(...)
}

Let me know if this helps!

Steffi

Hi Pedro,

Well if dfreq is giving you 12 measures, you'll want to change the code somewhat (because with only 10 spots in the data frame, if you try to insert 12 items the code will probably result in a warning). spec_param <- expand.grid(wave_file = "call.wav", call = temp_param$s, sample = 1:12,  time = NA, dfreq = NA)

    spec_param$time[spec_param$call == temp_param$s[i]] <- seq((cantos[i, 1]),(cantos[i, 2]), length.out = 10)

library(tuneR)
library(seewave)
s <- readWave("S.wav")

. Solution 1: to focus around the dominant frequency by using the function cutspec()
fspec <- spec(s, dB="max0", plot=FALSE)
fspec <- cutspec(fspec, flim=c(0,3))
Q(fspec)

. Solution 2: to compute the spectrum at a specific time position:
dfspec <- spec(s, at= 0.1, dB="max0", plot=FALSE)
Q(dfspec)

. Solution 3: to compute the meanspectrum:
mfspec <- meanspec(s, dB="max0", plot=FALSE)
Q(mfspec)

Solution 1 returns very different results than solutions 2 and 3 dues to the frequency resolution of the spectrum.

1) I've added spaces around = and <- and after , In general it easier to read a script if it's spaced out, but ultimately it's a matter of preference.
2) I've changed your cantos matrix to a cantos data frame. I think matrices might be computationally faster, but I find data frames easier to deal with and more intuitive, so for script clarity, I generally prefer to deal with data frames. And I changed the column names so they're more intuitive.
3) I've removed extra ( ). You only need () to group mathematical/logical operations or to define function arguments.

As you can probably, tell, none of these changes are bout turning "wrong" code into "right" code. In R you can achieve the same goal through many many different ways. I've merely put things in my style, because I find it a bit easier to follow and read, see if it works for you, if not, put it back to what you prefer!

I'm working with Melanie and I have encountered more problems with the Q function. messages.body_plain:
Hi Martin,

If I've understood you correctly, I think you just want to grab the output of spec and use R base graphics or a package like ggplot2 to make the figure. I think diffspec only shows you differences between

I would use meanspec instead of spec to grab the data, as I find the output of spec so large that it often overwhelms my computer when I try to plot :)

Here's an example using the two demo wavs from seewave. You can see the output of diffspec, base graphics and ggplot2. For base graphics and ggplot2, you can easily expand that to include more than two species. I've added commented out code to specify where you can add in more species, provided you have the meanspecs for them.

Enjoy!

Steffi

library(seewave)

data(tico)
data(orni)

# See the differences between spec and meanspec
spec(tico)
meanspec(tico)
spec(orni)
meanspec(orni)

# Save the data
t <- meanspec(tico, plot = FALSE)
o <- meanspec(orni, plot = FALSE)

# See the format the data is saved as
head(t)
head(o)

## Seewave Diffspec
diffspec(spec1 = t, spec2 = o, plot = TRUE)

## R base graphics
# Plot first species
plot(y ~ x, data = t, type = "l", xlab = "Frequency (kHz)", ylab = "Amplitude")

# Add other species to plot
points(y ~ x, data = o, type = "l", col = "blue")
#points(y ~x, data = third, type = "l", col = "red")

## ggplot2 graphics
library(ggplot2)

# Bind the rows from each spec together (rbind), but in each case first turn the data into a data frame and add a column specifying the species as a grouping factor for plotting
all <- rbind(data.frame(t, species = "tico"),
                   data.frame(o, species = "orni"))

#more than two species:
#all <- rbind(data.frame(t, species = "tico"),
#                   data.frame(o, species = "orni"),
#                   data.frame(x, species = "third"))
# etc.

# setup the plot, specifying species as a grouping variable
ggplot(data = all, aes(x = x, y = y, colour = species, group = species)) +
  theme_bw() + # For a white background
  geom_line() + # Plot the lines
  labs(x = "Frequency (kHz)", y = "Amplitude") # Fix the labels

Hi Martin,

If I've understood you correctly, I think you just want to grab the output of spec and use R base graphics or a package like ggplot2 to make the figure. I think diffspec only shows you differences between

I would use meanspec instead of spec to grab the data, as I find the output of spec so large that it often overwhelms my computer when I try to plot :)

Here's an example using the two demo wavs from seewave. You can see the output of diffspec, base graphics and ggplot2. For base graphics and ggplot2, you can easily expand that to include more than two species. I've added commented out code to specify where you can add in more species, provided you have the meanspecs for them.

Enjoy!

Steffi

library(seewave)

data(tico)
data(orni)

# See the differences between spec and meanspec
spec(tico)
meanspec(tico)
spec(orni)
meanspec(orni)

# Save the data
t <- meanspec(tico, plot = FALSE)
o <- meanspec(orni, plot = FALSE)

# See the format the data is saved as
head(t)
head(o)

## Seewave Diffspec
diffspec(spec1 = t, spec2 = o, plot = TRUE)

## R base graphics
# Plot first species
plot(y ~ x, data = t, type = "l", xlab = "Frequency (kHz)", ylab = "Amplitude")

# Add other species to plot
points(y ~ x, data = o, type = "l", col = "blue")
#points(y ~x, data = third, type = "l", col = "red")

## ggplot2 graphics
library(ggplot2)

# Bind the rows from each spec together (rbind), but in each case first turn the data into a data frame and add a column specifying the species as a grouping factor for plotting
all <- rbind(data.frame(t, species = "tico"),
                   data.frame(o, species = "orni"))

#more than two species:
#all <- rbind(data.frame(t, species = "tico"),
#                   data.frame(o, species = "orni"),
#                   data.frame(x, species = "third"))
# etc.

# setup the plot, specifying species as a grouping variable
ggplot(data = all, aes(x = x, y = y, colour = species, group = species)) +
  theme_bw() + # For a white background
  geom_line() + # Plot the lines
  labs(x = "Frequency (kHz)", y = "Amplitude") # Fix the labels
